content: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a disease associated with significant morbidity and mortality, and its global distribution continues to expand. It is the leading cause of tropical viral diseases. Currently, the majority of cases are reported from the WHO South-East Asia Region (approximately 60%) and the Western Pacific Region (about 40%). Most infections with the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) are asymptomatic or result in mild symptoms such as fever and headache. However, approximately 1 in 250 infections progresses to severe clinical illness. Severe cases are characterized by the rapid onset of high fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status or disorientation, coma, seizures (commonly observed in children), limb weakness, spastic paralysis, and, in many cases, death. The case fatality rate among symptomatic individuals can reach up to 30%, with an estimated 13,600 to 20,400 deaths annually. Among survivors, 20–30% experience permanent intellectual, behavioral, or neurological sequelae, including paralysis, recurrent seizures, and speech impairments. The causative agent of JE is the Japanese encephalitis virus, a member of the Flavivirus genus. The virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito, primarily of the Culex species. The incubation period ranges from 5 to 15 days. Humans are considered dead-end hosts and do not contribute to further mosquito transmission. The disease burden is significant, with an estimated 68,000 clinical cases occurring annually. JE is endemic in 24 countries across the WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions, placing over 3 billion people at risk of infection. The annual incidence of clinical disease varies widely across and within endemic countries, ranging from less than 1 to more than 10 cases per 100,000 population during outbreaks. While the virus primarily affects children, individuals of any age can be infected, although most adults in endemic areas develop natural immunity following childhood exposure. Vaccination is a critical preventive measure against JE. Four main types of JE vaccines are currently in use: 1. Inactivated mouse brain-derived vaccines: Production ceased in 2006, with limited remaining supplies. 2. Inactivated Vero cell-derived vaccines: Administered in two doses, four weeks apart, starting at >6 months of age in endemic settings. 3. Live attenuated vaccines (primary hamster kidney cell-derived): Administered as a single dose, starting at >8 months of age. 4. Live recombinant (chimeric) vaccines: Administered as a single dose, starting at >9 months of age. All current JE vaccines are derived from genotype III strains but elicit protective levels of neutralizing antibodies against other genotypes. Surveillance and laboratory diagnostics are essential for JE control. Diagnostic methods include IgM antibody detection, plaque reduction neutralization tests (PRNT), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and virus isolation. Specimens such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum are commonly used for testing. The WHO has developed comprehensive guidelines for JE surveillance and vaccination strategies, emphasizing the importance of strengthening laboratory networks and outbreak preparedness in endemic regions. Collaborative efforts among WHO, UNICEF, and other organizations aim to enhance JE control and prevention through vaccination programs, surveillance, and research.
